I. INTRODUCTION.
Despite the fact that the defendants, Julia Notarian and Charles Rossbach (jointly, "Defendants"), remain record the legal title holders of the property locate at 8127 Cedar Road, Chesterland, Ohio 44026 (the "Property"), the Estate of Anthony Notarian ("Plaintiff"), improperly seeks to evict them. Even more troubling is the fact that Plaintiff's alleged standing to evict is based on a non-final order from the Probate Court which is not subject to execution. Plaintiff's vindictive filing has the sole goal to effectuate a taking of the Property from Defendants to deprive them of their fundamental property rights and investment. Because there are genuine issues of material fact, Plaintiff's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment (the "Motion") should be denied.
II. FACTS.
In the Motion, Plaintiff states that the Property was transferred to Defendants in August of 2021 by Gino Notarian ("Gino").1 Gino held title to the Property since 2019, well
1 The Motion at Page 3.

before the death of Anthony Notarian ("Decedent").2 The Property is currently held by Defendants through a survivorship deed.3 Defendants secured a mortgage on the Property through Huntington National Bank. 4
In the Motion, Plaintiff states that "[i]n March of 2022 Judge Grendell granted partial summary judgment to the Estate of Anthony Notarian, ruling that the premises at 8127 Cedar Road be returned to the Estate, and ordering the Estate to manage any sale of the Premises."> It is noteworthy that the motion for partial summary judgment filed in the Probate Court relating to the Property, was filed prior to Defendants being named as parties, thus depriving them of the right to protect their interests. That notwithstanding, the Probate Court's ruling with regard to the Property is not a final order and cannot be executed upon.
The lack of a final order is evidenced by the ruling itself which does not contain the no just reason for delay language pursuant to Civil Rule 54(B). Additionally, the Probate Court's partial summary judgment order was subject to an appeal in which Plaintiff's counsel argued that said order was interlocutory and non-final by the filing of a motion to dismiss the appeal.6 Ultimately, the 11th District Court of Appeals dismissed the appeal ruling that the Judge Grendell's order was non-final.7
Despite seeking immediate possession of the Property, Plaintiff has taken no action to pay taxes or insure the Property.8 This despite Plaintiff's assertion that it owns the Property.9 Plaintiff also testified that Defendants could stay in the house if they bought it

III. LAW AND ARGUMENT.
A. Plaintiff Cannot Meet Its Burden Under Civil Rule 56(C) To Deprive Defendants Of Their Property Rights.
Rule 56(C) of the Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure provides that summary judgment may only be granted upon a trial court's determination that:
No genuine issue of material fact remains to be litigated; (2) The moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law; and (3) It appears from the evidence that reasonable minds could come to but one conclusion when viewing such evidence most strongly in favor of the party against whom the motion for summary judgment is made, that conclusion is adverse to that party.11
The standard for summary judgment requires that the court must construe the evidence most strongly in favor of the nonmoving party. Thus, the moving party may not make conclusory assertions that the nonmoving party has no evidence to prove its claim.12 The moving party must specifically point to some evidence of the type listed in Ohio Civil Rule 56(E) which demonstrates that the nonmoving party cannot support its claim. Upon satisfaction of this requirement, the nonmoving party must set forth specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.13
Based on the facts and the law, Plaintiff cannot meet the heavy burden of not only the granting of its affirmative claim but the denial of Defendants' right to present their defenses so that Plaintiff can effectuate what would be a judicial taking of their property.

Dresher v. Burt (1996), 75 Ohio St.3d 280, 662 N.E.2d 264.

B. The Court Cannot Grant Summary Judgment Based On A Non-Final Order Issued By The Probate Court.
Plaintiff argues that the Court should grant summary judgment based on the Probate Court's non-final order and rulings. For its Complaint, Plaintiff seeks to evict Defendants and also seeks money damages. These actions are in execution based on the Probate Court's non-final order and rulings. It is axiomatic that a trial court cannot execute on a judgment that is not final and appealable.14 In fact, "absent an express determination pursuant to Civ.R. 54(B), a judgment adjudicating fewer than all of the claims or parties does not terminate the action with respect to any party or claim, and that judgment is subject to revision throughout the remainder of the proceedings."15 Therefore, any such judgment is not subject to execution.16 Defendants' arguments in this regard are not novel as the case law relating to non-final orders is robust and long standing.17
Plaintiff attempts to bootstrap its argument by alleging that the deed executed by Defendants passes title to Plaintiff. This argument is disingenuous because the subject deed was ordered to be delivered and held by the Court. No control of said deed was given to Plaintiff. Furthermore, the deed was only signed when Defendants faced a contempt order based on the prior non-final order issued by the Probate Court. Therefore any argument in this regard are without merit.
14 The Farmers State Bank v. Steven Sponaugle, et al. (2017), 2017-Ohio-4322. See also, State ex rel. Electrolert, Inc v. Lindeman (1994), 99 Ohio App. 3d 154.
15 Id.
16 Id.
17 See Aselage v. Lithoprint, Ltd. (2009), 2009-Ohio-7036, Nwabara v. Willacy (1997), 1997 WL 186842, Wheeler v. Ohio State Univ. Med. Ctr. (2004) 2004-Ohio-2769.
4

IV. CONCLUSION.
In ruling on the Motion, this Court should be guided by the high standard under Civil Rule 56. The facts and law demonstrate that summary judgment is not appropriate as to the relief sought by Plaintiff based on a non-final order so as to deny Defendants' access to the Property and cause a taking. Accordingly, the Motion should be denied.

Procedural History
Ms. Scalzo is the duly appointed executrix of the Estate of Anthony Notarian. In July 2020 she filed an action for concealment and embezzlement of estate assets under R.C. 2109.50, and violations of R.C. Chapter 1337, in Geauga County Probate Court. Decedent's brother, Gino Notarian, was the initial defendant due to his actions as Anthony's power of attorney. The court referred the matter to mediation and
DEFENDANT'S EXHIBIT A

added Gino's daughter Liana as a party in October 2020. Following a period of discovery, Gino Notarian, Liana Gigliotti and Gino's son, Joe Notarian, testified under direct examination on March 20, 2021. The transcript of this examination was subsequently filed with the court.
Mediation sessions were held in the spring of 2021, but no settlement agreement was reached. On August 27, 2021, Ms. Scalzo filed a motion to protect estate assets and an amended complaint to conform to new evidence and to add parties. The trial court held the amended complaint in abeyance pending the report of a special master, and restrained the transfer of real estate in question. The special master issued a report recommending the return of real property to the estate in December 2021, and recommending the return of personal property in January 2022. The parties engaged in motion practice from September 2021 until the present, culminating in January 2022 with the entry of the amended complaint in the docket, and Ms. Scalzo's motion for partial summary judgment relating to real property assets of the estate.
In lieu of a competing motion for summary judgment, defendants Gino Notarian, Liana Gigliotti, and Joe Notarian filed a motion to enforce settlement, alleging agreements made in the context of mediation. The trial court denied the motion to enforce settlement, finding no agreement between the parties, and granted

Ms. Scalzo's motion for partial summary judgment. Gino Notarian, Liana Gigliotti, and Joe Notarian have appealed the granting of partial summary judgment and denial of -- the motion to enforce settlement.
Law
Appeals of right may be taken upon final dispositive orders. App.R. 4(A)(1). A final order may be one that affects a substantial right in a special proceeding. R.C. 2505.02(B)(2). An action for concealment and embezzlement is considered a special proceeding for purposes of R.C. 2505.02. Patrone v. Patrone, 2014-Ohio-5609, J 22, citing Swift v. Gray, 11th Dist. Trumbull No.2006-T-0106, 2007-Ohio-2302, J 7. "'Substantial right' means a right that the United States Constitution, the Ohio Constitution, a statute, the common law, or a rule of procedure entitles a person to enforce or protect." R.C. 2505.02(A)(1).
A special proceeding judgment only affects a substantial right when the nature of the judgment is such that a party could only obtain full and appropriate relief through immediate appeal. Patrone v. Patrone, supra, at J24, citing Jackson «. Herron, 11th Dist. No.2004-L-045, 2005-Ohio-4039, at J 8. "In other words, if the judgment in question does not result in the complete conclusion of the special

1
proceeding, it does not "affect' a substantial right if the relief a party could be given in an immediate appeal is identical to the relief obtained through an appeal at the close of the entire case." Swift o. Gray, 2007-Ohio-2302, J 7.
"When more than one claim for relief is presented in an action whether as a claim, counterclaim, cross-claim, or third-party claim, and whether arising out of the same or separate transactions, or when multiple parties are involved, the court may enter final judgment as to one or more but fewer than all of the claims or parties only upon an express determination that there is no just reason for delay." Civ.R. 54(B). With regard to concealment matters, for an order to be final, the court must make a finding of guilty or not guilty, and must make a determination with regard to the amount of penalty and attorney fees if requested. R.C. 2109.52.
Argument
By appellants' admission, the orders appealed from in the instant matter are interlocutory. See Appeal Docketing Statement, Page 2. Neither order awards a final monetary amount, calculates damages, or makes a determination on attorney fees, sanctions, or whether or not defendants are guilty of concealment. See Probate Court - Judgment Entry March 16, Page 9-10, Probate Court Judgment Entry March 13, page 7.

The orders do not contain Civ.R. 54(B) language indicating that there is no just reason for delay. Both orders contemplate further proceedings ("the real properties remain in contention and subject to further litigation," Id at 7), and in fact, the matter was scheduled for further proceedings on the motion of appellants when the matter was stayed for the appeal. On this basis, the appeal should be dismissed.
It also is difficult to ascertain what substantial right could have been affected by either order of the court. At no time have appellants argued the real property parcels in question are anything but estate assets temporarily held by Gino for the benefit of Anthony Notarian. Response to Complaint, J10, attached as exhibit A. It is implicit in appellants' motion to enforce settlement that the executrix is the proper person to make decisions regarding the disposition of the real property. In the absence of a written agreement signed by the parties, or a settlement agreement read into the court record, appellants do not have the right to purchase property from the estate at preferred terms to which Ms. Scalzo did not agree. Transferring the parcels to ! the Estate of Anthony Notarian does not affect any substantial right of appellants.
The court's summary judgment order makes clear further proceedings are necessary before the estate can dispose of the real property. The court provided 60 days from the date of entry during which appellants and occupants (who have not
.....

appeared in this appeal) could negotiate with the executrix regarding a potential sale or transfer of the Cedar Road parcel. Probate Court Judgment Entry March 16 at 9. All future real property transactions by the estate are subject to court approval. Id at 10. It is therefore impossible to argue appellants, or any other party, have had a substantial right affected. The court's orders are interlocutory in nature, with avenues appellants may avail at the probate court level. Accordingly, this appeal is not timely or appropriate, and Ms. Scalzo requests it be promptly dismissed, with jurisdiction over this matter returned to the Geauga County Probate Court.

On April 13, 2022, appellants, Gino Notarian, individually and as Trustee for the Gino Notarian Family Trust, Liana K. Gigliotti, individually and as Trustee for the Gino Notarian Family Trust, and Joe Notarian, filed an appeal from two entries: one denying their motion to enforce a settlement agreement and the other granting the motion for partial summary judgment filed by appellee, Maria Scalzo, and ordering certain real estate be returned to the probate estate.
{{2} The docket reveals that appellee, who is the executrix of the Estate of Anthony Notarian, filed an action against appellants for concealment and embezzlement.
DEFENDANT'S EXHIBIT

The matter was referred to mediation. Appellants filed a motion to enforce the settlement agreement, and appellee filed a motion for partial summary judgment. In a March 14, 2022 entry, the trial court found that no settlement agreement had been reached, and in a March 16, 2022 entry, the trial court ordered that 4 parcels of real estate be transferred back to the Estate of Anthony Notarian.
{3} On April 26, 2022, appellee filed a motion to dismiss the appeal for lack of a final appealable order. Appellee posits the appealed entries are interlocutory and contemplate further proceedings. Appellants filed a response in opposition to the motion to dismiss on May 18, 2022, alleging the orders are final because they were issued in a special proceeding and substantial rights were affected.
{[4} We must determine if there is a final order, as this court may entertain only those appeals from final judgments. Noble v. Colwell, 44 Ohio St.3d 92, 96 (1989). According to Section 3(B)(2), Article IV of the Ohio Constitution, a judgment of a trial court can be immediately reviewed by an appellate court only if it constitutes a "final order" in the action. Germ v. Fuerst, 11th Dist. Lake No. 2003-L-116, 2003-Ohio-6241, 1 3. If a lower court's order is not final, then an appellate court does not have jurisdiction to review the matter, and the matter must be dismissed. Gen. Acc. Ins. Co. v. Ins. Co. of N. Am., 44 Ohio St.3d 17, 20 (1989). For a judgment to be final and appealable, it must satisfy the requirements of R.C. 2505.02 and if applicable, Civ.R. 54(B). See Children's Hosp. Med. Ctr. v. Tomaiko, 11th Dist. Portage No. 2011-P-0103, 2011-Ohio-6838, 11 3.
{5} R.C. 2505.02(B) defines a final order as one of the following:
{[6} "An order is a final order that may be reviewed, affirmed, modified, or reversed, with or without retrial, when it is one of the following:
2
Case No: 2022-G-0019

281 or Sub. S.B. 80, or dealing with an appropriation proceeding. Therefore, R.C. 2505.02(B)(3)-(7) do not apply.
{118} Since this case involves a concealment action, it is a "special proceeding" for purposes of R.C. 2505.02(B)(2). Swift v. Gray, 11th Dist. Trumbull No. 2006-T-0106, 2007-Ohio-2302, 17. As such, any judgment issued could constitute a final appealable order if it affected any substantial right of appellants. Id.
{[19] R.C. 2505.02(A)(1) defines a "substantial right" as any right that a person is legally entitled to enforce under the United States Constitution, the Ohio Constitution, a statute, the common law, or a rule of procedure.
{[20} Although this matter involves a concealment action under R.C. 2109.50, the judgments on appeal did not affect a substantial right. Appellants may appeal the judgment once the Probate Court determines whether, and in what amount, restitution is owed and whether any rents or profits are owed on the assets that were kept from the estate. See In re Estate of Tewksbury, 4th Dist. Pike No. 05CA741, 2005-Ohio-7107, TT 11. Furthermore, the trial court has made no determination on the embezzlement claim. Thus, R.C. 2505.02(B)(2) does not apply.
{[21} Based on the foregoing, appellee's motion to dismiss is hereby granted. This appeal is dismissed for lack of a final appealable order.
{\22} Appeal dismissed.

THOMAS R. WRIGHT, P.J., concurs with Concurring Opinion.
{[23} I write separately to express my rationale for dismissal.
{124} "R.C. 2109.50 provides for a special statutory proceeding to discover concealed assets of an estate." Pirock v. Crain, 2020-Ohio-869, 152 N.E.3d 842, 11 64 (11th Dist.), citing In re Estate of Fife, 164 Ohio St. 449, 453, 132 N.E.2d 185 (1956). "When passing on a complaint made under section 2109.50 of the Revised Code, the probate court shall determine * * whether the person accused is guilty of having concealed, embezzled, conveyed away, or been in the possession of moneys, personal property, or choses in action of the estate * * " R.C. 2109.52. "If the person is found guilty, the probate court shall assess the amount of damages to be recovered or the court may order the return of the specific thing concealed or embezzled or may order restoration in kind." Id. "In all cases, * * * the probate court shall render judgment in favor of the fiduciary * * * against the person found guilty, for the amount of the moneys or the value of the personal property or choses in action concealed, embezzled, conveyed away, or held in possession, together with ten per cent penalty and all costs of the proceedings or complaint; except that the judgment shall be reduced to the extent of the value of any thing specifically restored or returned in kind as provided in this section." (Emphasis added.) Id.
5
Case No. 2022-G-0019
.

{[25} A judgment in a special proceeding, such as here, is final if it "affects" a substantial right. R.C. 2505.02(B)(2). An order "affects" a substantial right if it is "one which, if not immediately appealable, would foreclose appropriate relief in the future." (Citations omitted.) Bell v. Mt. Sinai Med. Ctr., 67 Ohio St.3d 60, 63, 616 N.E.2d 181 (1993). "To show that an order affects a substantial right, it must be clear that, in the absence of immediate review, the appellant will be denied effective future relief." (Citations omitted; emphasis sic.) In re Estate of Tewksbury, 4th Dist. Pike No. 05CA741, 2005-Ohio-7107, 1 10. "It is not enough that an order merely restricts or limits that right. Rather, there must be virtually no future opportunity to provide relief from the allegedly prejudicial order." (Citation omitted.) Id.
{\26} Here, the probate court's judgment granting partial summary judgment in favor of plaintiff does not constitute a final appealable order because it contemplates further action. First, it grants sixty days within which the executrix is to attempt to reach a settlement or resolution with the homeowners of certain real property belonging to the deceased's estate. Second, it makes appellant liable to the estate for any "rental income subject to these proceedings be returned to the estate," to be determined at the time the properties are returned to the estate. Therefore, the order does not include a specific monetary amount of damages. Third, the court orders "that any penalty associated with R.C. 2109.50, costs of the proceedings or complaint, including reasonable attorney fees, be determined at a later hearing date." "This is analogous to finding a party liable for damages but not determining the amount of those damages. Generally, this makes a judgment interlocutory." (Citations omitted.) Tewksbury at 1 10. More specifically, "the statute's penalty provisions are mandatory and, if a penalty is not imposed, no final order
6
Case No. 2022-G-0019

Wayne No. 09CA0062, 2010-Ohio-4065, 1 19, quoting Hawkins v. Innovative Property Mgt., 9th Dist. Summit No. 22802, 2006-Ohio-394, 1 5 (where the probate court failed to order the imposition of the mandatory statutory penalty relevant to concealment cases, the judgment failed to "contain a statement of the relief that is being afforded the parties"" and there was no final appealable order).
{[27} For these reasons, the probate court's judgment is not a final appealable order, and we are without jurisdiction to review this matter at the present time. Appellant may appeal the judgment once the probate court has determined the amount of damages and assessed the mandatory ten percent penalty, as stated in R.C. 2109.52. See Tewksbury at 1 14. Additionally, pursuant to the probate court's order of April 19, 2022, the transfer or conveyance of the real property to the estate, as well as of monetary/financial assets subject to the litigation, have been stayed pending this appeal.
{[28} Accordingly, I concur with the majority.
